transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Orion Head of AI), Daniel Ruiz (Orion Eng Mgr), Elena Markov (Orion Security)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood structured output / JSON mode and function/tool calling. Showed Console demo (schemas, guardrails), API examples, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Discussed security (SOC2, KMS, VPC) and next steps for a short POC.

Topics: structured output, JSON schemas, function calling, guardrails, security & compliance, POC scope, perf expectations

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is lena from Redwood, uh i'm with Marcus our solutions eng, we'll run through structured output and the function calling demo today, make it interactive so feel free to stop us
[00:18] Priya: hi thanks, excited — we've been evaluating a few vendors, want to see how Redwood handles strict JSON outputs for downstream pipelines
[00:29] Marcus: yeah great, that's the core of what we'll show — JSON mode with schema enforcement, plus the tool-calling ergonomics so you can map model responses into typed calls — we'll jump into the console in a sec
[00:40] Daniel: quick logistical Q: for the POC, we need to test on sample customer data. Any concerns about data residency or retention?
[00:49] Marcus: good question. For hosted we have configurable retention and optional data redaction; for Dedicated or Private you can retain zero logs and use KMS in your VPC or on-prem HSMs — we'll share the SOC2 and encryption docs after the call
[01:05] Elena: yes please send the SOC2, also which KMS integrations? AWS KMS, GCP CMEK?
[01:12] Lena: we support AWS KMS and GCP CMEK for Private, and we can integrate with customer KMS for Dedicated as well — Marcus will add the full list
[01:25] Marcus: (screen share) ok opening the Console — top-level here is Structured Output, we have JSON mode which lets you upload a JSON schema and the runtime will validate and either coerce or reject outputs based on your policy
[01:40] Marcus: so here's a sample schema for an invoice extraction: invoice_id string, total number, items array of objects with sku qty price — we'll show a few failure modes and guardrails
[01:56] Priya: in our pipeline the schema is strict, we can't accept missing fields. Can Redwood force strict validation?
[02:04] Marcus: yes you can set 'strict' vs 'coerce' policies. Strict will cause the call to return a structured_error and keep the raw text in an attachments blob. Coerce will attempt to coerce types and fill defaults. You can tune for leniency.
[02:18] Daniel: how is that enforced at inference time? Is it post-processing or baked into the model prompt?
[02:25] Marcus: it's a hybrid — we include the JSON schema in the prompt template (so the model is strongly guided), then we run a validator as a post-check. If the post-check fails and you have fallback policies it can retry with adjusted prompt or route to a more deterministic model variant or run a function to extract fields programmatically
[02:44] Priya: is that retry automatic? We don't want noisy retries causing duplicate downstream events
[02:50] Marcus: retries are configurable — you can set up a canary flow: on validation failure, first attempt a soft-rewrite prompt up to N times, otherwise return structured_error. There's also an 'auto-function-fallback' where a deterministic extractor runs as a tool call
[03:05] Marcus: speaking of tool calls, here's function-calling in action — we define functions in the API or via Console (name, params schema). The model can return a function call and Redwood will surface that to your app or optionally run the tool in the runtime if you supply the handler
[03:21] Lena: i'll show the live example: trigger a product search function with typed params, the model returns function_name and params JSON and we run the function, returning structured response to the user.
[03:34] (screen: code snippet) Marcus: example API flow: POST /v1/generate with schema param, mode=json, and a function definition for product_lookup with params {query, filters}. The model returns call to product_lookup with {query: "red running shoe", max_price: 100}. Redwood calls your webhook and returns the function result as a typed object
[03:58] Priya: can we restrict which functions the model can call? we have internal-only ops
[04:04] Marcus: yes — function whitelist per model/route; RBAC controls in the Console let ops specify allowed functions per API key or route. We also redact or mute sensitive fields by policy when passing to external webhooks
[04:20] Elena: how do you ensure the model doesn't hallucinate a function call or make up params?
[04:26] Marcus: the schema helps; plus our runtime validates the params against the declared param schema and rejects if mismatch. We also log the raw model decision so you can audit attempted calls — that's in the trace logs in Console
[04:41] Priya: what's the latency impact of schema enforcement and function middleware?
[04:46] Marcus: minimal for most workloads — the validator is fast. Worst-case rerun or fallback adds an extra roundtrip, but you can pin to a low-latency model variant or enable local deterministic extractors (that's what Dedicated/Private is for)
[05:00] Daniel: do you support streaming structured outputs? we want partial results as tokens come in
[05:07] Marcus: yes we support streaming with JSON pieces; we flush validated chunks and maintain a KV-ish cache for prefix state. Note sometimes streaming can complicate validation and we provide checksum based final validation hooks
[05:22] Priya: can you show an example where the schema fails and we do a fallback tool call?
[05:28] Marcus: sure — demo: ask for an order extraction, model returns malformed amount as string "one hundred" instead of number; post-validator fails, Console triggers a function 'normalize_amount' which calls a deterministic parser, we then merge and return a corrected typed object
[05:46] (Marcus types) [screen shows flow] Marcus: and you can see the trace: initial_response, validation_error, invoked_function(normalize_amount), patched_response — all logged with token-level latency and cost
[06:05] Elena: that's helpful. For compliance we need immutable audit logs with replayability — do you keep raw transcripts and the validator state?
[06:12] Marcus: yes we keep raw inputs, raw model outputs, validator results, function calls and responses. For Private deployments retention and immutability can be customer-managed. Audit logs are exportable via S3 or syslog depending on your deployment plan
[06:27] Priya: ok great — next, can we talk about guardrails and safety? we have customer PII and need redaction
[06:34] Marcus: we offer in-prompt redaction, post-process redaction, and a masking tool at call time; you can configure regex or ML detectors in the Console. For higher assurance we support in-line token masking before logs are written
[06:48] Daniel: for the POC we'll want both host options; maybe start hosted but Dedicated if perf or data isolation is needed. What's your typical TTD for Dedicated?
[06:57] Lena: Dedicated set up is usually a few weeks depending on capacity needs and contracts, Private/on-prem is longer — months — but we can run realistic benchmarks in hosted first, then port the workload to Dedicated for the committed phase
[07:12] Priya: about costing — how do you price function calls vs normal generation?
[07:17] Lena: function calls following a generation count as inline inference tokens plus a small per-call orchestration fee for managed webhooks. We also report token-level cost in the Console and Optimize will recommend batching and caching to reduce per-call unit costs
[07:31] Marcus: Optimize: here's the module — it analyzes request patterns and recommends batching windows, cache TTLs for K V cache, and quantization profiles for models based on your throughput and latency SLOs
[07:45] Marcus: for example, if you have lots of short chat turns we suggest smaller batch sizes and aggressive prefix caching; for high throughput extraction work we often recommend int8 quantization on Dedicated which gives big cost wins with minimal quality drop
[07:59] Priya: do you provide an eval harness to catch regressions when switching quantized models?
[08:04] Marcus: yes, Redwood Evals integrated in Console — you can pin a test set, run A/B and get quality regressions tied to prompts, we also support alerting when score drops below threshold
[08:18] (Pause) Lena: let's run a short live API example, Marcus will call the API from his laptop, we'll show the request/response and the Console trace
[08:30] Marcus: okay hitting the API now — request includes schema param and function definitions
[08:36] [08:36] Marcus (client): POST /v1/generate body={...schema... mode:json} 
[08:42] [08:42] Model: returns {"function_call": {"name": "product_lookup", "arguments": "{\"query\": \"red running shoe\", \"size\": 9}\"}}
[08:53] Marcus: Redwood invokes product_lookup webhook, webhook returns a typed array of matches, we surface structured payload back to the app. Latency here is 210ms end-to-end in the hosted region (us-west-2)
[09:05] Priya: that's excellent. Is 210ms median or p95?
[09:09] Marcus: that was p50 for this small payload — Console shows p50/p95/p99 breakdown and token costs per route
[09:19] Daniel: for repeatable benchmarks can we pin the model and access raw GPUs?
[09:24] Marcus: you can pin model version and variant. For Dedicated we give predictable GPU pools and you can request physical placement constraints; access to hardware-level metrics is available via our Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint
[09:38] Priya: any limitations we should know about on function calling — number of functions or param size?
[09:44] Marcus: practical limits exist (we recommend under 50 functions per route to keep prompt size manageable) and param payloads should be reasonably sized, but you can pass references (ids) and fetch richer objects server-side. We also support streaming function args if you need chunking
[09:58] Elena: security check: webhook auth patterns? we need mTLS to internal endpoints
[10:04] Marcus: we support mTLS for webhook delivery, signed JWTs, and VPC peering/private link options so webhooks never traverse public internet in Private/Dedicated setups
[10:18] Priya: can the Console restrict who edits schemas or adds functions? we need strict change control
[10:23] Lena: yes RBAC in Console, audit trail for config changes, and you can lock routes behind approvals. We'll show that in the Enterprise Admin settings in the follow-up demo
[10:36] Marcus: quick demo of guardrail policy editor: you can write rules like 'reject PII in param values' or 'require normalization for currency fields' — it's a rules engine attached to routes
[10:50] Daniel: great — last questions from our side: timeline for POC? success criteria?
[10:56] Priya: success looks like >=95% schema pass rate on our invoice extraction dataset, end-to-end latency under 300ms p95 for generation+function call, and clear security posture (SOC2 + KMS)
[11:09] Lena: understood. Proposed POC: 2 weeks hosted pilot using your sample dataset, we'll run evals and Optimize recommendations, then transfer to Dedicated if needed. We'll log results and propose a committed configuration if metrics meet thresholds
[11:24] Marcus: i'll own the tech setup and run benchmarks, lena will handle pricing/contract, and elena's security questions will be tracked — we'll share a short runbook after the call
[11:34] (PRIYA) Priya: sounds good. please include the example prompt sets and the test harness
[11:40] Lena: will do. any last questions?
[11:45] Elena: just one — is there a sandbox with synthetic data we can share with our compliance folks?
[11:50] Marcus: yes we have a demo org setup and synthetic dataset; we can spin up a sandbox project for Orion with expiring keys
[11:58] Lena: ok we'll follow up. thanks everyone for your time.
[12:03] (Call wrap) Lena: recap of next steps: send recording/slides, security pack, POC runbook, schedule benchmark meeting. We'll aim to start pilot next week.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings (K V cache -> KV cache, Webhook -> web hook) and speaker overlap — transcript minimally cleaned for readability.
